entry.title: Getting cross-track error right on WGS-84

link.title: Getting cross-track error right on WGS-84

entry.content:
A spherical estimate, a missing sign, and what 1,320 test cases taught me about turning geometry into code.

Given two waypoints and an aircraft position, I wanted the signed distance from the aircraft to the geodesic through those waypoints. The projection could fall before the start or beyond the end. I chose positive for the left side of the route and negative for the right.

The geometry fits on a page. The implementation needed much more care about direction, stopping conditions, and what an error measurement actually means.

A sphere makes a useful first estimate

On a sphere, the route lies in a plane through the Earth's center. A cross product gives the plane's normal; projecting the aircraft's unit vector onto that plane and normalizing it gives a nearby point on the great circle.

Earth is flattened at the poles. WGS-84 includes an ellipsoidal Earth model, so a spherical projection generally differs from the ellipsoidal one. For this implementation I used the direct and inverse geodesic formulas in Appendix E of RTCA DO-283C, the minimum operational performance standard for RNP area-navigation equipment. The spherical result became the initial estimate.

The solver

Let Q(s) be the point reached by traveling signed distance s from the start along the route. Negative distances extend behind the start. At Q(s), let α be the route's forward tangent bearing and β the bearing toward the aircraft. I solve the local perpendicularity condition:

f(s) = cosd(β(s) − α(s)) = 0

Here, cosd takes degrees. A point coincident with the aircraft is handled directly because its bearing to the aircraft is undefined.

  1. Compute the spherical estimate P₀, then convert its distance from the start into a signed initial distance s₀.
  2. Evaluate the actual ellipsoidal point Q(s₀). Accept it if the residual magnitude is at most 1e-4.
  3. Otherwise, start at s₀ ± 185 m. Use secant interpolation, replace the endpoint with the same residual sign, and use the midpoint if the denominator is zero or interpolation leaves the interval.
  4. Stop on the residual tolerance or a width of 0.001 m. After 20 iterations, return the remaining interval's midpoint and record that fallback separately.

This is a false-position update when the endpoints bracket a root. The final version uses a fixed interval without expansion.

An unsigned initial distance

An inverse geodesic returns a nonnegative distance. My along-route coordinate needed a sign. Without it, a projection 100 km behind the start becomes an estimate 100 km ahead.

I determine the sign from the angle between the start-to-P₀ bearing and the route's initial bearing. If their cosine is negative, I negate the distance. This selects the backward direction for the local initial estimate.

To isolate the effect, I reran test case 820 with only that correction disabled. The route runs east along the equator for 100 km. The aircraft is 10 km south of a reference foot 100 km before the start.

The unsigned interval never contained the foot. It still became narrow enough to stop, returning a cross-track distance of −200.435 km instead of −10 km. Restoring the sign let the initial residual check accept the correct foot without iteration. A small interval is useful evidence only when it encloses the intended solution.

Other details that changed the result

For the left/right sign, I initially considered the bearing from the projection to the destination waypoint. Beyond the destination, that bearing points backward; at the destination itself, it is undefined. Reusing the forward tangent bearing from the direct geodesic calculation fixes both cases. I also use one angle convention throughout: [−180°, 180°).

The tolerances have different units. A residual of 1e-4 is dimensionless; an interval width of 0.001 m is a distance. In one test, the initial residual passed even though the foot was 1.831 m from the reference. Its cross-track distance error was only about 0.091 mm. Accepting a small residual does not imply millimeter accuracy in the projected coordinates.

What I tested

The suite contains 810 combinations of six routes, 15 along-route positions, and nine lateral offsets, plus ten fixed cases and 500 seeded random cases. The combinations place the foot before the start, inside the segment, and beyond the end.

FactorCoverage
Start latitudeAbout −79.86° to +85°; both hemispheres and the equator
Route length1 m to 8,000 km
Distance outside either endpoint0.01 m, 100 m, and 1, 10, 100, 500 NM in the combination grid
Lateral offset0, ±0.01 m, ±1 m, ±1 NM, ±10 NM in the grid; no case exceeds 10 NM
Direction and longitudeNorthbound, eastbound, oblique routes, and longitude-wrap crossings

The random offsets were clipped to ±10 NM: 476 of the 500 landed on those boundaries. This part of the suite stresses the limit rather than sampling the interior uniformly.

Latest resultMeasured value
Cases passing the test criteria1,320 / 1,320
Initially opposite signs, among cases entering the loop953 / 953
Opposite signs in recorded iteration intervals3,119 / 3,119
Mean / maximum iterations2.363 / 20, including zero-iteration cases
Maximum cross-track distance error0.353 mm
Maximum projection-position error1.831 m, using the test's local coordinate-distance metric

Passing meant distance error below 2 mm, position error below 2 m, correct signs for nonzero offsets, and at most 20 iterations. The reference geometry shares the direct solver, so these are consistency tests. Seven standard reference cases and 30 independent geodesic ODE comparisons provide separate checks on the geodesic routines.

What this experiment taught me

I now treat the operating envelope as part of the algorithm: different latitudes, longitude crossings, and aircraft positions whose projections fall before, within, or beyond the route segment. A useful test suite also needs points on the route and extremely close to it. Ordinary mid-segment examples would have missed several of the problems here.

The secant formula is simple, but implementing it still means checking the conditions around it. For this interval-based variant, I verified that the initial endpoints had opposite signs, endpoint updates preserved that sign change, and successive intervals became smaller. These checks do not guarantee rapid convergence: one endpoint can remain fixed while progress slows. Convergence speed therefore needs its own checks against the iteration budget.

The objective function needs attention too. Near the route, the bearing toward the aircraft can change sharply as the candidate foot passes it. On the route itself, that bearing is undefined at coincidence, and the cosine residual can jump between opposite signs rather than smoothly reach zero. A residual-only stopping rule is therefore insufficient: coincidence handling and a justified positional stopping condition matter too. The secant denominator also needs its own zero check.

I would make angle ranges, bearing directions, signed distances, and units explicit at every interface. I would also choose tolerances from the required output accuracy, then measure function evaluations and runtime: tighter projection coordinates may cost more without materially improving cross-track distance. The 20-iteration limit bounds the outer loop, not total execution time or error. Every exit should say whether it met a tolerance or merely exhausted its budget. These tests support the cases measured; they do not prove convergence everywhere.
entry.summary: A spherical estimate, a missing sign, and what 1,320 test cases taught me about turning geometry into code.

entry.title: When AI Safety Evidence Stops Transferring

link.title: When AI Safety Evidence Stops Transferring

entry.content:
Frontier Al evaluation is moving beyond the model in isolation. Today’s frontier models can perform more complex tasks incorporating tools and context across longer horizons. Models plus the harness increasingly become the target of evaluations. The agent performance depends not only on the underlying model, but also on the harness. In one example, OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 performed materially better on cyber tasks when the harness preserved task-specific context over long trajectories (A shared playbook for trustworthy third party evaluations). Anthropic also recommends building a robust eval harness with a stable environment, as otherwise the eval results are unreliable, as demonstrated by seeing Claude gaining an advantage by examining the git history from previous trials (Demystifying evals for AI agents). Current evaluation practice is therefore becoming more configuration-aware. “Configuration” here means a specific combination of model and the harness under which behavior is evaluated. If evaluation results increasingly become configuration-dependent, how much can we still be confident in our pre-deployment eval results when configurations vary widely in everyday use? This question becomes more critical as agentic AI is deployed in safety-critical domains.

For example, in aviation, a change in the system may disqualify the system for being safe enough to deploy. This is because aviation takes a stricter view of configuration changes. SAE ARP4754A provides guidance for developing civil aircraft and systems. Its configuration management objectives cover system and item requirements, as well as facilities, tools, and data whose configuration is essential to demonstrating development assurance (§5.6.1(b)(1), (3)).

“Technical and administrative control of the configuration of: ... (4) Facilities, tools, and any other data necessary to support the development and verification activities.”

It also calls for a configuration baseline when requirements compliance substantiation is first sought (§5.6.1), with baseline establishment and subsequent change control addressed in §5.6.2.3(a)–(b).

“A baseline should be established for Configuration Items used for requirements compliance substantiation.”

Once established, the baseline should be protected, and subject to change control procedures (§5.6.2.3(b)). This ties the assurance evidence used to substantiate compliance and safety to a controlled configuration.

In practice, domain expert Leanna Rierson also recommends in her book, Developing Safety-Critical Software, A Practical Guide, that certain modification should trigger a change-impact analysis. The software must be re-verified on the intended target hardware and aircraft configuration before installation. Therefore in aviation, the transfer of assurance evidence from one configuration to another must be justified by rigorous impact analysis and re-verification where needed.

The same issue is beginning to appear in agent evaluation. Recent empirical work shows that agent capability can change substantially under different scaffolds. A controlled study on the GAIA benchmark compared 3 different scaffolds across 5 frontier models. It found that scaffold choice alone changed measured accuracy by a maximum of 28 percentage points for the same model. Together with the aforementioned OpenAI and Anthropic findings, they suggest that the configuration also determines the evaluation result. Yet these work largely examine how does the evaluation score changes when the scaffold changes. For safety-critical deployment, it is more essential to ask: If the scaffold changes, which parts of the previous approved safety evidence still hold, and which need to be re-established?

For instance, in aviation, Rierson notes two variables that affect the applicability of previous verification evidence: changes to the software itself, and changes to the environment in which the software is expected to operate. An agentic system is composed of multiple components, like memory, tools, and permissions, to name a few. If we apply the same logic to an agentic AI, we can reasonably infer that changing any of the above components may change the configuration itself and the operating envelope under which the agent was previously evaluated. The former is obvious. The latter is because changing a memory mechanism or adding a new tool or permission can not only affect the internal decision-making mechanism but also expand the action space and take the agent into new operational states. Borrowing change-impact analysis from aviation helps us answer the question raised in the previous paragraph.

Consider an AI agent deployed in an industrial setting. In the old configuration, the agent just reads sensor data and recommends future actions to a human operator. But the new configuration gives the agent permission to execute the action directly, holding the underlying model fixed. An impact analysis would inform us that since the safety implications of the behavior of the new configuration clearly change, previous evidence of operational safety may no longer be sufficient. Nonetheless, previous results of the model’s capability, like multi-run execution capability, may still be useful. A similar issue arises when giving the agent access to new tools or external systems in the new configuration that were not part of the original evaluation.

Future agentic AI evaluation needs to become more configuration-aware. Aviation provides a precedent for continuously updating complex airborne software systems while keeping the assurance evidence trustworthy. The same principle may be applied to AI and help continuously assess the compliance of safety objectives as agentic system evolves. Evaluation reports should clearly indicate the tested configuration, including the model, harness, and relevant environment. When any of the above elements changes through product iterations, a change-impact analysis could be added to the workflow and helps identify which parts of the previous safety evidence still hold. More research can be done to identify specific configuration changes that could significantly affect the system behavior and thus invalidates parts of previous safety evidence, for each specific vertical domain of application.
entry.summary: How configuration changes affect the validity of AI safety evidence, and what agent evaluation can learn from aviation assurance.
